attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post, relying on an unnamed source he says he confirmed with.

semantics.note: Faithful to both the no-ROI-tracking claim and the 'only purpose' inference. Leaving out the 'bad habits' clause does not change what is scored.

contract.note: The plain reading (no measure linking token use to useful output or cost, and leaderboard climbing as the sole purpose) is ordinary. It correctly says that absence from public reporting does not prove internal absence.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous report confirming the Claudeonomics leaderboard. It does not show whether separate ROI tracking existed. It also mentions an adoption aim, which does not settle the question of sole purpose.
Company disclosure of output-per-engineer gains for an earlier period. It does not tie output to token cost or to the April leaderboard.
Secondary summary of WSJ and a Meta spokesperson: a separate AI Insights dashboard tracks usage more holistically. The measures are not identified, and ROI tracking is not shown.

reviews.rationale: The leaderboard is corroborated. Whether Meta had any ROI-style measure, and whether climbing the leaderboard was the sole purpose, is not settled. The AI Insights dashboard is described too vaguely to count as an ROI measure. Nothing in the packet confirms the claimed absence of tracking.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: A compound claim: a present exclusive-cause claim about popularity plus an unhedged 'will be seen' forecast with no deadline. The revised wording keeps all the elements.

contract.note: The support and contradiction conditions track 'only', 'incremental', 'too expensive' and 'bloated' at their ordinary strength. The early-resolution bar is appropriately high for 'in the end'.

evidence.note: Early-2025 trial found a 19% slowdown for experienced developers. One snapshot, which METR itself now calls out of date. Not evidence of the eventual outcome.
METR's 2026 follow-up suggests likely speedups and that developers decline to work without AI. METR says its own data is weak because of selection effects. Not decisive.
Field experiments involving the companies found about a 26% increase in completed tasks, mostly for less experienced developers. Different tasks and setting; does not resolve the eventual forecast.

reviews.rationale: 'In the end' sets no deadline, and the early-resolution rule needs a decisive, broad body of evidence. The studies point in mixed directions. None of them isolates the causes of adoption, full costs, or long-term code bloat, so the forecast cannot yet be scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Combines a present claim, an impossibility claim and a 'will never' claim. The scope is the 'fantastical' agents he describes, not basic web automation.

contract.note: The minimal reading (any agent completing some multistep live-web tasks) is stretched against him. His next sentence admits Operator exists but 'does not work', so 'do not exist' cannot mean basic web agents. The contract itself notes 'fantastical' implies stronger, unspecified capabilities.

evidence.note: Dated June 2026 preprint with released code: 51% success on live-site tasks. It would contradict only the minimal reading. It does not show the 'fantastical' agents the speaker was talking about.
BrowserArena (2025) documents brittle open-web agents. It cannot show permanent impossibility.

reviews.rationale: The claim targets 'fantastical' internet agents, and in context he concedes that basic web agents exist but do not work. The contract's minimal existence test does not match those words, and the stronger capability he denies is never defined. A 51% benchmark agent therefore cannot fairly decide the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The API-migration premise is something he says he heard but could not confirm.

semantics.note: Correctly keeps the unconfirmed antecedent ('this' means the reported forced API migration) together with the usage mandates. The causal effect itself is stated firmly ('naturally increases').

contract.note: Requiring the antecedent to be established before testing the cost effect is fair. condition_status 'not_applicable' sits oddly with a claim that carries an explicit condition, but the support condition does require the antecedent.

evidence.note: Sept 2026 report: Anthropic announced, then paused, separating agentic and API use in subscriptions. It does not confirm that enterprise clients were forced onto the API, and it gives no per-engineer cost comparison.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent (providers forcing enterprises onto API billing) is still unconfirmed. The only evidence shows a pricing change that was announced and then paused. With the antecedent unknown and no employer-level cost data, the causal claim cannot be scored.
